text: Miya Masaoka (born 1958, Washington, D.C.) is an American composer, musician, and sound artist active in contemporary classical and experimental music. Her work includes contemporary classical composition, improvisation, electroacoustic music, inter-disciplinary sound art, sound installation, traditional Japanese instruments, and performance art. She is based in New York City and has performed on a 21-string Japanese koto, extended through software processing, string preparations, and bowing. She has created performance works and installations that incorporate plants, live insects, and sensor technology. Her full-length ballet was performed at the Venice Biennale in 2004. She has received the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Fellowship (2021), the Doris Duke Award (2013), the Herb Alpert Award (2004), and a Fulbright Fellowship for advanced research in Noh, gagaku, and the ichi gen kin. She is an associate professor in the MFA Visual Arts Department at Columbia University and the director of the MFA Sound Art Program. Masaoka began studying classical music at age eight. In her early 20s, she moved to Paris, France, and after returning to the U.S., enrolled at San Francisco State University, where she earned a BA in Music, magna cum laude, studying with Wayne Peterson and Eric Moe. She holds an MA from Mills College, where she received the Faculty Award in Music Composition, with teachers including Alvin Curran, Maryanne Amacher, and David Tudor. Her work spans voice, orchestra, installations, electronics, and film shorts, and includes handmade responsive garments (LED KIMONO) and pieces mapping insect movement, plant responses, and brain activity to sound (Pieces For Plants, The Sound of Naked Men, Thinking Sounds). Her works have been commissioned and premiered by Bang on a Can, So Percussion, Either/Or, Kathleen Supove, Joan Jeanrenaud, SF Sound, Volti, Rova Saxophone Quartet, Alonzo King’s Ballet, The Del Sol String Quartet, and others. Her orchestral work “Other Mountain” was selected for a reading by JCOI Earshot for the La Jolla Symphony in 2013. She founded and directed the San Francisco Gagaku Society (1989–1996) under Master Suenobu Togi, a former Japanese Imperial Court musician whose gagaku lineage traces back over 1000 years to the Tang Dynasty. Her interest in nature and resonant outdoor spaces led her to record migrating birds in the canyons near the San Diego Airport, resulting in “For Birds, Planes and Cello,” written for Joan Jeanrenaud. “While I Was Walking, I Heard a Sound” is scored for 120 singers, spatialized in balconies of a concert hall, with one movement featuring three choirs and nine opera singers making bird calls and environmental sounds. As a kotoist, she has performed and recorded with Pharoah Sanders, Pauline Oliveros, Gerry Hemingway, Jon Rose, Fred Frith, Larry Ochs, Maybe Monday, Steve Coleman, Anthony Braxton, Reggie Workman, Dr. L. Subramaniam, Andrew Cyrille, George E. Lewis, Jin Hi Kim, Susie Ibarra, Vijay Iyer, Myra Melford, Zeena Parkins, Toshiko Akiyoshi, William Parker, Robert Dick, Lukas Ligeti, Earl Howard, Henry Brant, and others. Masaoka describes herself as deeply moved by the sounds and kinetic energy of the natural world, emphasizing the complexity and fundamental nature of human heartbeat, lunar rhythms, oceanic cycles, and cultural soundscapes. She initiated and founded the San Francisco Electronic Music Festival in 1999. In 2004, she received the Alpert Award in the Arts, and previously received a National Endowment for the Arts award and a Wallace Alexander Gerbode Award. The New York Times describes her solo performances as exploring the extremes of her instrument, and The Wire describes her compositions as magnificent, virtuosic, and essential. She has been a faculty member at the Milton Avery Graduate Program at Bard College in Music/Sound since 2002 and has taught music composition at NYU. She received the Doris Duke Performing Artist Award in 2013 and a Fulbright Scholarship for Japan in 2016. Her recorded works include: Myths, Modes and Means (BMG/RCA, 1996), What We Live (Black Saint, 1996), Suite for Koto and Jazz Orchestra (BMG, 1997), Twelve Minor (Avant, 1998), Global Fusion (Erato, 1999), Trancepatterns (Dendroica Music, 2000), Burdocks (Tzadik, 2001), Legends and Legacies (Asian Improv Records, 2005), Cloud Plate (Cryptogramophone, 2005), Sequel (for Lester Bowie) (Intakt, 2006), Sound Body (samadhisound, 2007), and With Fred Frith and Maybe Monday.
